items.answer: adat

items.stem: Distinguish between the Minangkabau rumah gadang and the Nayar taravad.
items.answer: Both are matrilineal households holding property through women, but the taravad was managed by a senior man and largely dissolved after legal reforms, while the rumah gadang remains symbolically central and women control ancestral land.
items.markingKey: Both are matrilineal households holding property through women, but the taravad was managed by a senior man and largely dissolved after legal reforms, while the rumah gadang remains symbolically central and women control ancestral land. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why the Nayar taravad declined in the twentieth century.
items.answer: Colonial and post-independence laws allowed partition of taravad property and recognised conjugal marriage, while education, wage employment and reform movements among Nayar men favoured nuclear households and fathers' responsibility for their children. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Colonial and post-independence laws allowed partition of taravad property and recognised conjugal marriage, while education, wage employment and reform movements among Nayar men favoured nuclear households and fathers' responsibility for their children. items.stem: "In matrilineal societies fathers have no role." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Fathers often have important emotional, ritual and economic roles; Trobriand fathers nurtured children and gave gifts, though children belonged to the mother's dala.
items.markingKey: Fathers often have important emotional, ritual and economic roles; Trobriand fathers nurtured children and gave gifts, though children belonged to the mother's dala. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the rumah gadang, the carved wooden longhouse with roofs like buffalo horns, only Ibu Yusnimar's elderly aunt still lives full-time. Her daughters work in Padang and Jakarta and return for Idul Fitri. This year the family discussed selling a rice field to pay for repairs. Yusnimar's brother, the mamak, said he would decide; his nieces said the field was theirs. In the end, the women agreed to lease the field rather than sell it. "Land given by the ancestors is not for sale," Yusnimar said, "but we are not farmers any more."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a Minangkabau village in West Sumatra, Indonesia.

Discuss the ethical issues an anthropologist would need to consider when carrying out the fieldwork described in the text. Suggest how the anthropologist might respond to the dilemmas you identify.

items.stem: Lars writes: "Matrilineal systems inevitably disappear with modernisation." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Some decline (Nayar) while others adapt and persist (Minangkabau, Akan), depending on law, property and religion.
items.markingKey: Some decline (Nayar) while others adapt and persist (Minangkabau, Akan), depending on law, property and religion. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain how Malinowski's Argonauts of the Western Pacific illustrates the concept of power. Refer to the people, place and time of the ethnography.
items.answer: Holding famous kula valuables and keeping many partners brings renown; chiefs and successful kula men gain status through generosity, so prestige rather than accumulation underpins influence.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Holding famous kula valuables and keeping many partners brings renown; chiefs and successful kula men gain status through generosity, so prestige rather than accumulation underpins influence. Explain how the text shows matriliny adapting to social change, using one or more anthropological concepts. Distinguish between what the text shows and what you infer from it.
items.answer: Migration to cities and non-farming work weaken daily use of matrilineal property, but women's ownership of ancestral land is reaffirmed; the mamak's claim and the nieces' response show negotiation between male authority and female ownership; leasing rather than selling is an adaptation preserving inalienable ancestral property while responding to economic change.

items.stem: "Social relations is central to understanding matriliny and social change." Compare and contrast two anthropological studies, for example Gough's study of the Nayar and Sanday's Women at the Center, in the light of this claim.
items.answer: Gough's study of the Nayar (on the Nayar of Kerala, south India, as they lived before twentieth-century legal reforms): Nayar girls underwent a tali-tying rite before puberty; later they could take several visiting sambandham partners, while children belonged to their mother's matrilineal household (taravad). Sanday's Women at the Center (among the Minangkabau of West Sumatra, Indonesia (fieldwork from 1981)): Houses, land and lineage pass through women; men traditionally migrate (merantau) and hold authority as mother's brothers (mamak) in their sisters' lineage. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far social relations is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

items.answer: Kinship by birth is based on descent and shared substance; kinship by practice is created through feeding, co-residence, care and choice.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that kinship is better understood as something people do than as something people are born into? Answer with reference to one ethnography in depth.
items.answer: Both are true: kinship is given by birth and descent and also continually made through practice.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: relatedness through feeding (Carsten), chosen families (Weston), swapping networks (Stack); descent determines membership and property in many societies (Nuer, Minangkabau); birth-based kinship carries legal and religious weight (Kahn). items.answer: Both show kinship created through everyday sharing – rice on Langkawi, food and childcare in "The Flats" – but in very different conditions (a Malay fishing village versus urban poverty in the US), showing how practice-based kinship responds to context.

items.answer: Kinship distributes property, authority and care unequally by gender and age; comparing who controls resources (karanavan vs. Minangkabau women) reveals how kinship organises power.

items.stem: Explain the difference between alliance theory and descent theory.
items.answer: Descent theory (Radcliffe-Brown, Fortes, Evans-Pritchard) explains social organisation by descent groups; alliance theory (Lévi-Strauss) explains it by marriage exchange between groups.
items.markingKey: Descent theory (Radcliffe-Brown, Fortes, Evans-Pritchard) explains social organisation by descent groups; alliance theory (Lévi-Strauss) explains it by marriage exchange between groups. items.stem: With reference to a comparison of Gough and Sanday, explain how it illustrates matriliny and change.
items.answer: Both describe matrilineal societies, the Nayar of Kerala and the Minangkabau of West Sumatra. The Nayar taravad was dissolved by law and reform, while Minangkabau matriliny adapted, showing how property, religion and law shape outcomes.

items.stem: Compare and contrast Evans-Pritchard's The Nuer and Stack's All Our Kin as accounts of kinship and social organization compared across two ethnographies, focusing on the key concept of social relations.
items.answer: Evans-Pritchard's The Nuer (among Nuer cattle pastoralists of the Upper Nile, southern Sudan (fieldwork 1930–1936)): Political order rested on segmentary lineages that united against more distant groups and divided when conflict arose within, giving order without a state. Stack's All Our Kin (among poor African American families in "The Flats", a pseudonymous neighbourhood of a Midwestern US city (late 1960s)): Networks of kin and "fictive" kin swapped goods, childcare and money, so domestic groups stretched across several households as a survival strategy. items.stem: Distinguish between modernisation theory and an anthropological view of change.
items.answer: Modernisation theory sees societies moving in a single direction from traditional to modern, extended to nuclear families; anthropologists show change as uneven, reversible and shaped by local agency and global inequality.

items.stem: With the help of a specific example, explain why change in social organisation is not simply "modernisation".
items.answer: Change is uneven and can reverse (Ferguson's Copperbelt); people combine new and old forms (WhatsApp clans, transnational households), so linear models of progress from extended to nuclear families do not fit. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.)

Every Lunar New Year, the village in Sichuan fills up with cars from Chengdu and Shenzhen. Grandmother Liu has raised her granddaughter Xiaomei since she was two, while Xiaomei's parents work in a phone factory. This year Xiaomei, now twelve, refused to go with her parents to the city for the holiday visit. "Grandma is my home," she said. Her mother cried in the car. On the village wall, a faded slogan still reads: "Fewer births, better births."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a village in Sichuan, China.

Explain how the text illustrates change in social organisation caused by migration and the state, using one or more anthropological concepts. Make clear which key concept you are using and why it is relevant.
items.answer: Rural–urban labour migration (and hukou restrictions that make it hard to raise children in cities) produces left-behind children raised by grandparents, so care and attachment shift across generations ("Grandma is my home"); the household is stretched between village and city; the slogan recalls state fertility policy shaping family size.

items.stem: Compare and contrast how change is shown in Peggy Levitt, The Transnational Villagers (2001) and James Ferguson, Expectations of Modernity: Myths and Meanings of Urban Life on the Zambian Copperbelt (1999).
items.answer: Levitt's The Transnational Villagers (among migrants from Miraflores, Dominican Republic, and their community in Jamaica Plain, Boston): "Social remittances" – ideas, behaviours and identities – flowed from Boston to Miraflores, changing gender roles, politics and religious practice in the village. Ferguson's Expectations of Modernity (among mineworkers on the Zambian Copperbelt during the economic decline of the 1980s): When copper prices collapsed, the promised path to urban modernity reversed; many mineworkers returned to rural areas, undermining linear stories of progress. Similarities and differences should be made explicit, e.g. how far change is imposed by wider structures or negotiated by the people themselves in each context, and how the methods and theoretical approach of each ethnographer shape the account.

In the rumah gadang, the carved wooden longhouse with roofs like buffalo horns, only Ibu Yusnimar's elderly aunt still lives full-time. Her daughters work in Padang and Jakarta and return for Idul Fitri. This year the family discussed selling a rice field to pay for repairs. Yusnimar's brother, the mamak, said he would decide; his nieces said the field was theirs. In the end, the women agreed to lease the field rather than sell it. "Land given by the ancestors is not for sale," Yusnimar said, "but we are not farmers any more."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a Minangkabau village in West Sumatra, Indonesia.

items.answer: Migration to cities and non-farming work weaken daily use of matrilineal property, but women's ownership of ancestral land is reaffirmed; the mamak's claim and the nieces' response show negotiation between male authority and female ownership; leasing rather than selling is an adaptation preserving inalienable ancestral property while responding to economic change.

In the refugee settlement, the Abdi household is made up of people from three different families. Every Lunar New Year, the village in Sichuan fills up with cars from Chengdu and Shenzhen. Analyse how the text illustrates change in social organisation caused by migration and the state. Support your answer with evidence from the text. Use appropriate anthropological terminology throughout your answer.
items.answer: Rural–urban labour migration (and hukou restrictions that make it hard to raise children in cities) produces left-behind children raised by grandparents, so care and attachment shift across generations ("Grandma is my home"); the household is stretched between village and city; the slogan recalls state fertility policy shaping family size.

items.answer: The research was requested by the Anglo-Egyptian Sudan government after Nuer resistance to colonial rule, raising questions about anthropology's colonial uses.

items.stem:
Read the text below.

In the rumah gadang, the carved wooden longhouse with roofs like buffalo horns, only Ibu Yusnimar's elderly aunt still lives full-time. Her daughters work in Padang and Jakarta and return for Idul Fitri. This year the family discussed selling a rice field to pay for repairs. Yusnimar's brother, the mamak, said he would decide; his nieces said the field was theirs. In the end, the women agreed to lease the field rather than sell it. "Land given by the ancestors is not for sale," Yusnimar said, "but we are not farmers any more."
— Original ethnographic extract written for this question bank (fictional composite): fieldnotes from a Minangkabau village in West Sumatra, Indonesia.

Compare and contrast how change is experienced by the people in the text and by the people in one other ethnography you have studied (for example Annette Weiner, Women of Value, Men of Renown: New Perspectives in Trobriand Exchange (1976)). Make sure you contextualise the ethnography: author, people, place and time.
items.answer: Text: Migration to cities and non-farming work weaken daily use of matrilineal property, but women's ownership of ancestral land is reaffirmed; the mamak's claim and the nieces' response show negotiation between male authority and female ownership; leasing rather than selling is an adaptation preserving inalienable ancestral property while responding to economic change. Ethnography – Annette Weiner, Women of Value, Men of Renown: New Perspectives in Trobriand Exchange (1976), in Kiriwina, Trobriand Islands, revisiting Malinowski's field site in the 1970s: Her restudy shows how anthropological knowledge changes: a male ethnographer's access shaped what was recorded, and a later female ethnographer revealed women's exchange. Comparison: similarities and differences in how change is produced, expressed or contested in the two settings, with explicit links between them.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Comparing kinship across societies shows more differences than similarities."
items.answer: Differences in form are striking, but comparison reveals common functions and processes.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: descent systems, residence and marriage vary widely. Arguments against: all societies use kinship to organise care, belonging and property; similar processes of making kin through sharing appear in very different places. Supported judgement: Differences in form are striking, but comparison reveals common functions and processes. Markbands (10 marks): IB SCA Paper 2 markbands scaled to the marks: top band – focused argument, detailed and contextualised ethnography (author, people, place, time), key concepts and theory used critically, reasoned conclusion; middle band – relevant ethnography and some analysis but partly descriptive; lower band – generalised, little ethnographic support.
